newsitem.title: Japan: No alternative to France's deficit cutting - Chirac.
newsitem.headline: No alternative to France's deficit cutting - Chirac.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac said on Tuesday that France had no alternative to its current austere economic and budgetary policies and he was prepared to accept the deep unpopularity they have caused.
Speaking on a state visit to Japan, he said measures to cut public sector deficits would be implemented in full, despite widespread opposition, but could probably be explained better.

"This has a high political cost for the government. But there is no other route if we really want to serve our country and get over our difficulties," he told Japan's Keidanren employers' association.
"So we have to accept the negative reaction of public opinion and probably try to explain things better."
Opinion polls show Prime Minister Alain Juppe's public approval rating has fallen to about 25 percent, while support for Chirac has slipped to around 35 percent.
Public hostility has prompted sniping at Juppe within the ruling centre-right coalition and rumours of a possible cabinet reshuffle or even a change of prime minister.
Political sources expect Juppe to stay, at least until next year and possibly until the 1998 general election.
However, Chirac's talk of the need to explain policy better may be seen as a veiled criticism of the government.

But an aide said the president dismissed with a hand gesture rumours in parliament in Paris of a cabinet reshuffle as early as next weekend, with Finance Minister Jean Arthuis and Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre being replaced.

The rumours suggested two supporters of ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur -- former budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy and former justice minister Pierre Mehaignerie, now chairman of the parliamentary finance committee -- would join the cabinet.
"Reforms always worry people, especially in difficult times but...if we don't reform the causes of these anxieties, we'll never make it," Chirac said.
"We have to show our willpower and shoulder responsibility, even if that is unpopular," he said.
France had got into bad budget habits over decades and the government should not be afraid to confront "public opinion which prefers talk of reform to the reality", he said.

Contrary to French political tradition, in which the prime minister acts as a lightning rod for the president, Chirac has been forced to come publicly to Juppe's rescue three times since the summer recess, reaffirming his support in reaction to attacks on the premier within the coalition.

In his Tokyo speech, Chirac said the state was "much too omnipresent, much too paralysing" in the French economy. He blamed the nationalisation policies of his Socialist predecessor, the late Francois Mitterrand.
But he said France intended to preserve the special status of public services despite European pressure for greater competition.

"That is why we have difficulties with the European Union, which wants to liberalise public services. France will make no concession in this area. It is extremely attached to the French concept of public service, in which each citizen has the same rights wherever he lives," Chirac added.
